Categories.value: PD NASA|Featured pictures of Sicily|Featured pictures on Wikipedia, Spanish|Etna in 2018|Satellite pictures by Landsat 8|2018 eruptions in Italy|Italy photographs taken on 2018-12-28|December 2018 in Sicily|Featured pictures of volcanoes|Featured photographs in the public domain|Flank eruptions|Satellite pictures of Etna in 2018|Satellite pictures of Mount Etna eruptions

ImageDescription.value:
For the first time in perhaps a decade, Mount Etna experienced a “flank eruption”—erupting from its side instead of its summit—on December 24, 2018. The activity was accompanied by 130 earthquakes occurring over three hours that morning. Mount Etna, Europe’s most active volcano, has seen periodic activity on this part of the mountain since 2013.

The Operational Land Imager (OLI) on the Landsat 8 satellite acquired the top image of Mount Etna on December 28, 2018. The second image highlights the active vent and thermal infrared signature from lava flows, which can be seen near the newly formed fissure on the southeastern side of the volcano. The image was created with data from OLI (bands 4-3-2) and the Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS) on Landsat 8.

Ash spewing from the fissure cloaked adjacent villages and delayed aircraft from landing at the nearby Catania airport. Earthquakes occurred in the subsequent days after the initial eruption and displaced hundreds of people from their homes, according to news reports.

Artist.value: NASA Earth Observatory images by Joshua Stevens, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Text by Kasha Patel.

ImageDescription.value:
Volvo PV544 B18 (built in 1961) in the parking lot of the barbecue area in Merfeld, Dülmen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
The Volvo PV 544 was a further development of Volvo’s PV series and was built from 1958 to 1965. It replaced the PV 444 and retained its characteristic rounded pontoon shape in the style of the 1940s.
With the introduction of the B18 engine in the early 1960s, the PV 544 was equipped with a modern 1.8-liter four-cylinder engine with an overhead camshaft. Depending on the model, it delivered between 75 and 90 hp. The engine was considered robust and durable, which contributed significantly to the model’s good reputation.
The PV 544 was known for its solid workmanship, high safety standards (including early three-point seat belts) and reliability. It also enjoyed success in rallying, for example in international long-distance rallies.
By the end of production in 1965, over 440,000 units had been built.
